Chapter 5: Humility and the Willingness to Change at the Peak of Success
You know, hitting the top of your career feels incredible. It's like all those years of hard work finally pay off, and you get this wave of validation. But here's the twist—when you’re at your best, that’s actually when it gets tricky. Why? Because you’ve got to stay open to change, even if the world around you is telling you you’re doing everything right.
That takes a special kind of humility. And I’m not talking about selling yourself short or pretending your achievements don’t matter. Real humility is about knowing there’s always room to grow, no matter how much you’ve accomplished. It means you’re willing to listen, willing to learn, and ready to adapt—even if it’d be so much easier to just sit back and enjoy the glory.
But let’s be honest—complacency is a sneaky trap. Success can make you feel untouchable, like your way is the only way that works. And once you start thinking like that, you shut out new ideas and fresh perspectives. Suddenly, it gets a whole lot harder to keep up when things start to shift.
Think about a seasoned athlete. No matter how many trophies are on the shelf, they know staying at the top means always training, learning from coaches and teammates, and adjusting to new rivals. That same mindset works in any profession. The most effective leaders? They stay curious. They invite feedback. And they see change as something constant, not a one-time event.
Another part of humility is giving credit where it’s due. Nobody climbs the ladder alone. Colleagues, mentors, teammates—everyone plays a part. When you recognize that, you build trust and create a collaborative, supportive culture that lifts everyone up.
Now, being willing to change is closely tied to resilience. Change isn’t always comfortable. Sometimes it means leaving your comfort zone and facing your own limitations. But if you walk into that space with humility, you’re better prepared to handle setbacks—and you’ll keep growing, no matter what.
So, how do you actually put this into practice? Here are a few ideas:
Start by regularly asking for input from a wide range of colleagues. Take time to reflect on your own blind spots and areas for growth. Show gratitude for the people who help you along the way. Be open to new ideas, even if they challenge what you already believe. And when change feels uncomfortable, remind yourself—it’s a chance to learn something new.
When you make humility a habit, you create a space where getting better is just part of the culture. Not only do you become more effective, you set the tone for everyone around you.
So, if you remember one thing from this chapter, let it be this: The fifth step in growing is to nurture humility and that willingness to change—even when you’re at the very top. Stay open to feedback, celebrate the people who help you succeed, and keep embracing the adventure of learning and adapting.
